title: Unlocking Tensor Core Performance for Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA and EPFL show that Tensor Core FP32 emulation (BF16x9 on Blackwell via cuBLAS, TF32x3 on Ampere via CUTLASS) speeds up the Point Edge Transformer interatomic potential without retraining: up to 2.5x on GEMMs and 1.7x per MD step on B300, and up to 1.9x/1.5x on A100. TF32x3 preserves FP32-like energy conservation and relaxation convergence, whereas one-pass TF32 is faster but drifts and fails to converge.

insights.claim: Many machine learning interatomic potentials still run inference in FP32 because force errors accumulate over molecular dynamics timesteps, leaving the much higher low-precision Tensor Core throughput of modern NVIDIA GPUs unused.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Scientific AI workloads represent untapped GPU performance that software alone can unlock, extending installed-base value.

insights.claim: Tensor Core FP32 methods split each FP32 operand into lower-precision components, compute cross-products on Tensor Cores and recombine them with FP32 accumulation, giving near-FP32 accuracy without retraining or changing weights or architecture.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Emulated precision lets NVIDIA trade FP32 silicon for low-precision Tensor Cores while still serving HPC and science customers.
insights.quote: This approach can increase matrix-multiplication throughput while retaining accuracy close to native FP32, without retraining or changing the model’s weights or architecture.

insights.claim: On Blackwell GPUs, cuBLAS BF16x9 decomposes each FP32 operand into three BF16 components and recombines nine pairwise products, and can be enabled for PyTorch GEMMs via the CUBLAS_EMULATE_SINGLE_PRECISION=1 environment variable with no model-code changes.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: A zero-code-change switch lowers adoption friction and strengthens CUDA software lock-in on Blackwell.

insights.claim: In matrix-multiplication tests against an FP64 reference, BF16x9 matched or exceeded native FP32 accuracy, supporting its use as a drop-in FP32 GEMM replacement, while TF32x3 has a slightly different accuracy profile needing workload-specific validation.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Suggests native FP32 hardware may matter less for future GPU generations if emulation matches it.
insights.quote: BF16x9 matched or exceeded native FP32 accuracy against an FP64 reference, supporting its use as a drop-in replacement for FP32 GEMMs on supported hardware.

insights.claim: With BF16x9 on Blackwell, large GEMMs in the Point Edge Transformer sped up 2.2-2.5x for a 17,280-atom system and 1.2-1.4x for a 192-atom system, with error below the model's own non-determinism.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Software-delivered speedups on already-optimized GEMM workloads raise effective throughput per Blackwell GPU for science customers.
insights.quote: Importantly, the error due to the BF16x9 Tensor Core method is below the model’s own level of non-determinism.

insights.claim: End-to-end molecular dynamics step speedups with BF16x9 were 1.7x (performant) and 1.4x (eager) on the 17,280-atom system and 1.2x and 1.1x on the 192-atom system.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: End-to-end gains are well below kernel gains, a reminder to discount kernel-level marketing numbers.

insights.claim: On A100, TF32x3 accelerated PET's major GEMMs by 1.7-1.9x and the full MD step by up to 1.5x, while keeping force error to roughly three times the run-to-run FP32 difference.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Ampere installed base gains usable life for scientific workloads through software updates.

insights.claim: For the 255M-parameter large PET checkpoint on a 192-atom system, TF32x3 gave a 1.4x speedup versus 1.2x for the 26M small checkpoint, with force error of 3.9 × 10⁻⁶ eV/Å essentially unchanged.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Larger models benefit more from GEMM acceleration, implying growing returns as scientific foundation models scale.

insights.claim: PET was chosen as a demanding test because it already spends much of its runtime in highly optimized GEMMs, so BF16x9 exposed performance headroom without retraining, architecture changes or custom kernels.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Even well-optimized scientific codes leave GPU performance on the table, favoring NVIDIA's library-level optimization strategy.

insights.claim: One-pass TF32 achieves higher raw speedups than TF32x3 but introduces visible roughness in the CO/Pt(111) potential-energy curve and larger systematic energy drift in NVE water simulations, whereas TF32x3 matches FP32 behaviour.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Naive low-precision speedups can produce physically wrong results, which favors validated emulation paths over the fastest mode.

insights.claim: In relaxing a 539-atom Cantor-alloy slab with FIRE2 in the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit, TF32x3 converged in 218-222 steps versus 218 for FP32 at a 1.5x per-step speedup, while one-pass TF32 (2.0x per step) failed to converge even within 1,000 steps.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Per-step speed is meaningless if convergence fails; time-to-solution is the right metric for materials-discovery compute.
insights.quote: One-pass TF32 achieved a 2.0x per-step speedup but failed to converge even after doubling the optimization step limit to 1,000 steps.
insights.locator: TF32x3 accelerated each optimization step by 1.5x

insights.claim: End-to-end gains from Tensor Core FP32 methods scale with system size and GEMM share of runtime; small systems benefit less because launch overhead, neighbor processing and graph operations dominate.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Large-system simulations are where GPU emulation delivers value; small-molecule workloads remain overhead-bound.
insights.quote: End-to-end gains depend on system size and the share of runtime spent in GEMMs.

insights.claim: The authors recommend evaluating Tensor Core FP32 methods on other MLIPs and precision-sensitive scientific ML models dominated by large FP32 GEMMs, as an independent performance layer stackable with CUDA graphs, fused ops and custom kernels, though combined gains were not measured.
insights.speaker: Anoushka Bhutani
insights.so_what: Points to a broader push of emulated FP32 into scientific computing as NVIDIA's chemistry/materials stack (ALCHEMI) expands.
